source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5240584, read in full in my own browser tab (abstract, introduction, methods, results with Tables 1-5, discussion, acknowledgments, footnotes, affiliations, references). The PMC text is an author manuscript (NIHMS818095) of JAMA Psychiatry 2015;72(8):757-766, not the publisher's version; locators follow the manuscript. The online supplement (eTables 1-4) was not read.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of the figures taken from this paper. Three wording points: (1) 'diagnosed with a structured interview given by lay interviewers': this paper names the structured interview (AUDADIS-5) but never says the interviewers were lay people (Grant et al. 2017 says they were not clinicians). (2) The 2013 NSDUH 7.0% is, in this paper's framing, a DSM-IV figure, so comparing it with the DSM-5 13.9% mixes definitions; against the NESARC-III DSM-IV 12-month figure (12.7%) it is 55%, still about half (editors' calculation). (3) The closing inference ('these studies cannot show whether the disorder became more common') is the editors' appraisal. This paper supplies its main premises (differences in survey methods; NSDUH stable at about 7.5%; a call for research into the discrepancy), but its authors still describe the DSM-IV change as a substantial increase. The claim should say that the authors read it as a real increase.
claims.note: Every DSM-5 number in the statement and magnitude that comes from this paper is correct: 13.9 (0.31); 7.3 (0.19), 3.2 (0.13), 3.4 (0.12); lifetime 29.1 (0.48) with 8.6, 6.6 and 13.9; men 17.6 and women 10.4; lifetime men 36.0 and women 22.7; ages 26.7, 16.2, 10.0 and 2.3; 36,309; 72.0, 84.0 and 60.1%. Recomputed: 7.3+3.2+3.4 = 13.9; 8.6+6.6+13.9 = 29.1; the mild share is 7.3/13.9 = 52.5% (unweighted 2624/5133 = 51.1%), so 'about half' holds. 7.0/13.9 = 50.4%. Nonresponse 39.9% ('4 in 10'). The printed screener and person rates multiply to 60.5%, not 60.1%; this is immaterial here. 'Partly' refers only to the trend sentence (see overstatement); all the figures are supported. Funding: NIAAA and NIDA, NIH grant K05AA014223 and the NIAAA intramural programme; 10 of 11 authors are at NIAAA's Laboratory of Epidemiology and Biometry, and Westat was the field contractor; conflicts: none reported. So 'which also ran the survey' is accurate, although the paper's role-of-funder statement says the funders had no role in design, conduct or analysis.

anchors.locator: Methods > Sample, 1st paragraph; Abstract > Design, Setting, and Participants
anchors.extracted: Face-to-face interviews; target population US noninstitutionalized civilian adults aged 18+ including residents of selected group quarters (e.g. group homes, workers' dormitories); multistage probability sampling with Hispanic, black and Asian oversampling; 36 309 respondents; screener-level response 72.0%, person-level 84.0%, total 60.1%; data April 2012 to June 2013.

anchors.locator: Results > Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 1st paragraph; Table 2, Total row
anchors.extracted: 12-month DSM-5 AUD 13.9% (SE 0.31), lifetime 29.1% (0.48). 12-month mild 7.3 (0.19), moderate 3.2 (0.13), severe 3.4 (0.12); lifetime mild 8.6 (0.18), moderate 6.6 (0.18), severe 13.9 (0.31). Unweighted n: 12-month any 5133 (mild 2624, moderate 1186, severe 1323); lifetime 10 001. Weighted percentages.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Sex and Age rows; Table 3, Sex and Age rows
anchors.extracted: 12-month AUD men 17.6 (0.42), women 10.4 (0.34); lifetime men 36.0 (0.62), women 22.7 (0.53). 12-month by age 18-29 26.7 (0.74), 30-44 16.2 (0.55), 45-64 10.0 (0.32), 65+ 2.3 (0.22). Adjusted OR (all other sociodemographic characteristics) men vs women 1.9 (1.72-2.01); age 18-29 vs 65+ 13.9 (11.57-16.67).

anchors.locator: Methods > Diagnostic Interview, 1st paragraph; Methods > Alcohol Use Disorders, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Diagnoses from NIAAA's structured AUDADIS-5 interview. DSM-5 AUD requires 2+ of 11 criteria; severity mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe 6+ criteria. Test-retest kappa for the DSM-5 AUD diagnosis 0.60-0.62 (dimensional ICC 0.83-0.85). Against blind clinician reappraisal (PRISM-5), diagnostic agreement was fair to good (kappa 0.49 and 0.62), dimensional ICC 0.81-0.85. The paper does not say the interviewers were lay people.

Published US estimates are DSM-IV based. 2001-2002 NESARC: 12-month 8.5%, lifetime 30.3%. NCS-R: 4.4% and 18.8%, lower because of a skip rule that missed cases. 2013 NSDUH 12-month AUD 7.0% (ref. 16); no explanation of the NSDUH difference is offered.

anchors.locator: Results > Prevalence, Onset, and Sociodemographic Correlates, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: DSM-IV AUD in NESARC-III 12.7% (12-month) and 43.6% (lifetime) vs 8.5% and 30.3% in 2001-2002, which the authors call a substantial increase and link in part to more heavy drinking (unpublished: 5+ drinks/day 31.0% to 39.6%). NSDUH 12-month AUD stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013 (cited as ref. 15, a 2004 NESARC paper; the citation looks wrong). The authors call for research into the increase and the discrepancies between surveys.

DSM-IV symptom items nearly identical in NESARC and NESARC-III (3 reworded, 3 abuse questions added). NESARC-III DSM-IV 12-month AUD with and without the added questions: 12.7% and 12.2% (kappa 0.98). The authors' check that item changes did not produce the rise.

Weighted for oversampling and screener- and person-level nonresponse, post-stratified to the 2012 American Community Survey; the authors report that weighting compensated adequately for nonresponse. Respondents vs the full eligible sample: no difference in Hispanic, black or Asian share or segment-level traits; slightly more men (48.1% vs 46.2%) and people aged 60-69 (13.7% vs 12.6%).

Limitations: some survey methods differed between the 2001-2002 NESARC and 2012-2013 NESARC-III. Homeless people, prisoners and most treated people were not covered, so estimates may underestimate true AUD prevalence. Cross-sectional design.

anchors.extracted: Funded by NIAAA and NIDA, NIH grant K05AA014223 (Hasin) and the NIAAA intramural programme. Ten of 11 authors at NIAAA's Laboratory of Epidemiology and Biometry; Westat was the NESARC-III contractor. Conflicts: none reported. claims.overstatement: Two wording points, no overstatement of the figures. (1) 'which would lower its figures': the paper says the missing groups (homeless people, prisoners, most treated people) may make AUD prevalence too low. Applying this to help-seeking is the editors' inference; it is plausible, since most treated people were not covered, but 'would' is firmer than the paper's hedged wording. (2) 'such as Alcoholics Anonymous' is the editors' example; the paper names only 12-step groups. 'Sought treatment or help', self-reported, matches the paper, and the abstract's wording is 'ever treated'.
claims.note: All numbers checked against Results > Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD: 7.7 and 19.8; DSM-IV 8.1 and 15.6 (2001-2002: 7.2 and 14.0); by severity, 12-month 2.7, 4.9 and 21.3 and lifetime 4.4, 8.7 and 34.7; sources 4.5, 3.6, 2.0 and 1.8; lifetime rehabilitation 9.0 and practitioners 8.7; age at first treatment 29.4 vs onset 26.2 (a 3-year lag). Response 60.1%. Other sources of help are only in eTables 3-4 of the supplement, which was not read. The paper does not give the time frame of help-seeking for the 12-month group. Its discussion attributes the low treatment rate to stigma and beliefs that treatment does not work (citing other studies, not NESARC-III data). The claim omits this, which is acceptable. Funding and conflicts as in the prevalence claim.

anchors.locator: Results > Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Of respondents with 12-month and lifetime DSM-5 AUD, 7.7% and 19.8% sought treatment or help for AUD. DSM-IV: 8.1% and 15.6%, vs 7.2% and 14.0% in the 2001-2002 NESARC. Mean age at first treatment 29.4 years vs mean onset 26.2 years.

anchors.locator: Results > Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 12-month AUD: help from 12-step groups 4.5%, health care practitioners 3.6%, outpatient facilities 2.0%, rehabilitation programmes 1.8%; other sources less frequent (supplement eTables 3-4). Lifetime AUD: rehabilitation 9.0% > practitioners 8.7%. Help-seeking rose with severity: 12-month 2.7%, 4.9%, 21.3%; lifetime 4.4%, 8.7%, 34.7% (mild, moderate, severe).
The abstract reports the 19.8% lifetime figure as the share of respondents with lifetime AUD who were 'ever treated'; the results section calls it seeking treatment or help.
Household survey including selected group quarters; 36 309 respondents; total response 60.1% (screener 72.0%, person 84.0%).
Homeless people, prisoners and most treated people not covered, so AUD prevalence may be underestimated (stated for prevalence, not specifically for help-seeking). Cross-sectional survey.

key_findings.correction: Editors' SD arithmetic rechecked: severe vs none 0.52-0.76 SD, mild vs none 0-0.19 SD.

reporting_issues.note: 5.2/1.8 = 2.9 and 16.1/1.5 = 10.7, so the factor of about 3 to 11 is right.
The Results > Comorbidity text makes the same across-severity statement.
No cell of Table 4 reads 1.2 (1.01-1.43); specific phobia with moderate lifetime AUD is 1.2 (1.01-1.54).
Checked in the page markup: no bold elements or bold-styled cells in any table. Table 4 has a superscript c with only footnote a defined.
Recounted: Social Functioning has 8 of 11 unmarked (1-4 and 6-9 criteria), Role Emotional 5 of 11 (1-4 and 9 criteria); Mental Health and the Mental Component Summary are all marked.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall moderate (JBI) is reasonable. One detail: domain 6 and the exposure field say the interviewers were lay people, which this paper does not state. Grant et al. 2017 does (Limitations: interviewers were not clinicians).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is fair: the headline figures are faithful and the errors are in the abstract. One location fix: item (7) puts the 3-year onset-to-treatment lag in the Discussion, but it is in Results > Seeking Treatment or Help for AUD, 1st paragraph.

missed: Citation error (Discussion, 1st paragraph): the statement that NSDUH 12-month AUD was stable at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013 is cited to ref. 15 (Hasin and Grant, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2004, a NESARC paper on abuse and dependence), which cannot support a 2002-2013 NSDUH trend. The figure is the authors' statement without a checkable source here; a reporting issue should record this, because the claim relies on the figure.

Unsourced card wording: the design detail says 'computer-assisted interviews' and the outcomes field says 'diagnoses generated by computer algorithm'. Neither paper (this one or Grant et al. 2017) says this; the text names the AUDADIS-5 and field methods only. Remove these details or give a source.
